name: Vistra Corp.

profile.description: Vistra Corp. is an integrated retail electricity and power generation company operating approximately 44,000 MW of generation capacity across natural gas, nuclear, coal, solar, and battery storage facilities. The company serves approximately 5 million retail customers and owns the second-largest competitive nuclear fleet in the United States, including the Comanche Peak Nuclear Plant in Texas and PJM nuclear facilities acquired through Energy Harbor. Vistra achieved investment grade credit ratings at two major agencies in 2026.

innovation.label: STRONG
innovation.analysis: Track Record (3/3): CEO Jim Burke executed two transformative acquisitions — Energy Harbor (2024) and Lotus (2025) — that repositioned Vistra from a legacy coal/gas utility to a strategic AI infrastructure provider, with 20-year PPAs signed with Meta (2,600+ MW nuclear) and Amazon locking in decades of premium pricing [1][2]. This pivot fundamentally changed the company's investor narrative and growth trajectory. AI Deployment (1/2): Vistra deploys AI internally for grid optimization and predictive maintenance across its ~44,000 MW fleet, but AI is a demand driver rather than a product — the company supplies power to AI data centers, not AI products to customers, and no specific AI-driven cost savings have been quantified [2]. Market Share (2/2): Vistra operates 6.4 GW of nuclear capacity — the second-largest competitive nuclear fleet in the U.S. — and serves ~5 million retail electricity customers, giving it a dual position as both a baseload power provider and retail distributor [1][2]. Pipeline (1/2): Plans for two new 860 MW natural gas units in West Texas, nuclear uprate opportunities, and 20-year license extensions for Comanche Peak and Perry plants (into the 2050s) provide growth visibility, but the pipeline is incremental capacity expansion rather than transformative new products [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): Utility-sector R&D intensity is inherently low; Vistra invests in operational technology but not at levels that distinguish it from peers.

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Vistra's purpose — 'lighting up lives, powering a better way forward' — is clear and connects power generation to human impact and progress, supported by specific commitments to 60% CO2 reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050 [3]. However, the purpose was recently articulated as part of a corporate rebrand and has not been validated by decades of consistent execution; it remains a standard-tier utility mission. Community Impact (1/2): Vistra serves 5 million retail customers and was recognized as a Texan 20 honoree for community engagement, but two fires at the Moss Landing battery storage facility in Monterey County (2024 and 2025) caused community evacuations, environmental contamination with heavy metals and asbestos, and ongoing health concerns that undermine community trust [4]. Employee Retention (1/2): Burke's 'One Team' integration culture across the Energy Harbor and Lotus acquisitions and the safety-first culture essential for operating a six-reactor nuclear fleet suggest organizational stability, but no specific retention metrics, turnover rates, or average tenure data are publicly available [2]. Insider Buying (0/2): CEO Burke has been a consistent net seller of VST shares throughout 2025-2026, with documented sales totaling approximately $60M+ including $17.2M in October 2025, $9.1M in September 2025, $8.7M in October 2025, and $4.09M in November 2025 [7]. While many of these were tied to pre-planned stock option exercises, there is no evidence of meaningful open-market insider buying by the CEO or other executives.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Vistra's financial profile has strengthened materially since the prior screen. Q1 2026 delivered operating revenues of $5.64B (up 43.5% YoY) and net income of $1.029B versus a loss of $268M in Q1 2025, driven by higher realized capacity prices and full-period Lotus acquisition contributions [1]. ROE surged to 42.9% (well above the 15% target), profit margin improved to 11.52% (up from 5.3%), and Forward P/E of 17.45 is attractive for a company guiding to $6.8-7.6B in 2026 EBITDA [1][6]. The Forward PEG of 0.38 is exceptional, reflecting consensus EPS growth expectations of ~46% and making VST one of the most attractively valued growth stories in the market. D/E of 355% remains well above the 300% floor and scores 0 on this metric, reflecting the capital-intensive utility model and acquisition-driven growth. TTM revenue of $19.45B represents ~12% growth on a trailing basis, with 5-year revenue CAGR of approximately 10% [6]. The company reaffirmed 2026 adjusted FCFbG guidance of $3.925-4.725B and was upgraded to investment grade by a second major credit rating agency [1]. Liquidity floor cleared easily at ~$893M daily traded value.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Vistra is structurally immune to AI disruption and is one of the primary beneficiaries of AI buildout — every hyperscale data center requires 24/7 baseload power, and Vistra's 6.4 GW nuclear fleet provides exactly that [1][2]. The company's 20-year PPAs with Meta (2,600+ MW nuclear) and Amazon lock in decades of AI-driven demand at premium pricing, and U.S. electricity demand continues to grow driven by data center expansion. Physical power generation is the ultimate AI-immune business — AI cannot generate electrons, and no amount of software innovation replaces the need for reliable baseload electricity. Nuclear license extensions into the 2050s ensure these assets will serve AI demand for decades [2]. AI Opportunity (1/1): Vistra generates direct, quantifiable revenue from AI infrastructure through long-term nuclear PPAs with hyperscalers. Q1 2026 operating revenues of $5.64B (up 43.5% YoY) were partially driven by contracted data center power deliveries, and the company is in active discussions with additional data center operators to increase nuclear power output [1][2].

infinite_game.summary: Vistra under Jim Burke demonstrates meaningful infinite game qualities — the transformative Energy Harbor and Lotus acquisitions to pivot toward nuclear/AI infrastructure, the 20-year PPA strategy that prioritizes long-term revenue visibility over short-term pricing flexibility, and the commitment to emissions reduction all suggest a company playing to endure. However, the purpose is recently articulated rather than battle-tested, continued operation of heavily polluting coal plants alongside clean energy ambitions creates tension, and the Moss Landing battery fires raise questions about operational execution on the sustainability front.

just_cause.analysis: Vistra's evolving purpose of 'lighting up lives, powering a better way forward' connects its work to a genuine societal need — providing reliable, affordable, increasingly clean power to enable the AI and clean energy transitions [2][3]. The pivot from coal-heavy legacy utility to nuclear-powered AI infrastructure provider represents real strategic alignment with a larger purpose. However, the cause is partially lived rather than fully validated — Martin Lake coal plant remains one of the nation's worst polluters, the Moss Landing battery fires exposed gaps in operational execution, and the purpose statement was recently articulated as part of a corporate rebrand rather than proven through decades of consistent execution [4][5]. (2 points)

trusting_teams.analysis: Burke's 'One Team' integration philosophy across the Energy Harbor and Lotus acquisitions demonstrates genuine commitment to organizational cohesion rather than a divide-and-conquer approach [2]. The safety-first culture essential for operating a six-reactor nuclear fleet requires high-trust teams — nuclear plant operations literally cannot function without psychological safety, procedural discipline, and empowered workers willing to raise concerns. However, rapid integration of multiple acquisitions inherently creates organizational disruption, and no specific employee satisfaction, retention, or turnover data is publicly available to confirm the culture claims. (1 point)

worthy_rivals.analysis: Vistra acknowledges Constellation Energy as a worthy rival in nuclear power for AI data centers, and management's competitive response has been to improve their own offering — signing competitive PPAs, pursuing nuclear uprates, and securing 20-year license extensions — rather than focusing on defeating or disparaging the competition [1][2]. The competitive dynamic with Constellation has pushed both companies to innovate in nuclear-AI partnerships, reflecting an infinite competitive mindset. (1 point)

existential_flexibility.analysis: The Energy Harbor and Lotus acquisitions fundamentally repositioned Vistra's identity from a legacy coal and gas power generator to a nuclear-powered AI infrastructure provider — a genuine strategic evolution driven by the energy transition rather than desperation [2]. The company is also diversifying from coal to gas/nuclear/solar/battery storage, showing willingness to transform the generation mix. However, Vistra did not abandon its legacy business entirely (coal and gas plants still operate) and the changes, while significant, are additive rather than a true 'blow up the existing model' reinvention in the Sinek mold. (1 point)

courage_to_lead.analysis: Burke took the bold step of acquiring Energy Harbor's nuclear fleet and signing 20-year PPAs at a time when nuclear energy was politically controversial, betting that nuclear would become essential for AI data center baseload power before this thesis was consensus [1][2]. The commitment to $4.3B+ in annual capex for fleet expansion and optimization, plus a share repurchase program that has retired roughly 30% of outstanding shares since 2021, demonstrates willingness to invest heavily for long-term capability. However, the nuclear-for-AI thesis has since become market consensus, and the massive share repurchases — while creating shareholder value — also boost near-term EPS rather than representing a purely courageous long-term sacrifice. (1 point)

investment_thesis: Vistra delivered a breakout Q1 2026 with operating revenues of $5.64B (up 43.5% YoY) and net income of $1.029B versus a loss of $268M a year earlier, driven by higher realized capacity prices and full-period Lotus acquisition contributions [1]. The company reaffirmed 2026 EBITDA guidance of $6.8-7.6B and adjusted FCFbG of $3.925-4.725B, was upgraded to investment grade by a second major credit agency, and trades at a Forward P/E of 17.45 with a PEG of 0.38 — making it one of the most attractively valued AI-adjacent growth stories in the market [1][6]. The 20-year nuclear PPAs with Meta (2,600+ MW) and Amazon provide exceptional revenue visibility, and Vistra's 6.4 GW nuclear fleet with license extensions into the 2050s positions it as a durable beneficiary of the structural increase in U.S. electricity demand driven by AI data center buildout. ROE of 42.9%, profit margin of 11.52% (up from 5.3%), and ~30% share reduction through buybacks demonstrate improving capital efficiency and shareholder alignment.
thesis_continued: The bear case centers on leverage, environmental liabilities, and insider selling. D/E of 355% is elevated even after improvement, reflecting $19.93B in total debt against only $658M in cash, which leaves limited financial flexibility if power prices decline or interest rates remain elevated [6]. CEO Burke has been a consistent net seller of VST shares, with approximately $60M+ in stock sales during 2025-2026, suggesting the CEO may view current valuations as extended despite the compelling growth narrative [7]. The Moss Landing battery storage facility fires in 2024 and 2025 caused community evacuations, environmental contamination with heavy metals and asbestos, and triggered an EPA federal response action — creating ongoing regulatory and litigation exposure [4]. Martin Lake coal plant remains one of the nation's top sulfur dioxide and mercury polluters, carrying forced-retirement risk from tightening EPA regulations [5]. Nuclear operational risk persists — an unplanned outage at Comanche Peak or PJM facilities during contracted PPA periods would create material financial penalties and reputational damage.
key_catalysts: Full-year realization of 20-year Meta and Amazon nuclear PPAs plus additional hyperscaler PPA signings, driving EBITDA toward the high end of the $6.8-7.6B guidance range with premium contracted pricing [1]
Investment grade credit upgrade enabling lower borrowing costs and potential debt refinancing, improving free cash flow conversion on the $19.93B debt load [1]
Nuclear uprate opportunities and 20-year license extensions for Comanche Peak and Perry plants ensuring multi-decade cash flow visibility as AI data center power demand continues to accelerate [2]
key_risks: Elevated leverage at 355% D/E with $19.93B total debt and only $658M cash leaves minimal financial flexibility if power prices decline or if integration of recent acquisitions generates unexpected costs [6]

Environmental and litigation exposure from two Moss Landing battery storage facility fires (2024-2025) that triggered EPA federal response action, community evacuations, and heavy metal contamination — plus ongoing regulatory risk from operating Martin Lake, one of the nation's top polluters [4][5]
Consistent insider selling by CEO Burke (~$60M+ in 2025-2026) signals potential management concern about current valuation levels despite the compelling AI-power growth narrative [7]
